fields.connection: V/A plain form + ではないか / N・Na + ではないか
examples: Isn't that a little dangerous?
Hasn't he already gone home?
Isn't that great! Let's go with this plan.
Being late — isn't that questionable for a working adult?
Everyone, let's reconsider this once more.
I think he may be busy.
fields.explain:
Rising intonation at the end of the sentence → asking/inviting agreement; falling intonation → exclamation, criticism, praise.
のではないか is more objective/softer than the direct ではないか.
V-ようではないか is used in speeches and rallying calls; in everyday life it is replaced by ～よう（よ）/ ～ようか.
じゃないか is versatile: agreement, criticism, dissatisfaction, praise depending on the context.

• Rhetorical question/affirmation seeking agreement: “Isn't it…?”, “Wouldn't it be…?”. High degree of certainty; the speaker wants the listener to agree.
• Emphasis of emotion (praise/disapproval/criticism): the voice falls at the end of the sentence, making it an exclamation: “That's good!”, “It's already late!”.
• Suggestion/call to action (V-ようではないか): “Let's …!”. Speech or slogan style.
• Formality: ではないか (formal/written) > じゃないか (spoken language). The form のではないか is used when a long clause serves as the subject.
fields.notes:
• In journalism and editorials, ではないか is often used to lead an argument and call on readers to agree.
• んじゃないか (contracted form of ＝のではないか) is common after verbs/adjectives: 難しいんじゃないか.
• Avoid repeating では: with N/なA + のではないか you need “なの”: 静かなのではないか.
• Using じゃないか in complaints can easily sound aggressive; consider the relationship and intonation.
mistakes: Confusing it with だろう: ではないか seeks agreement or expresses exclamation; だろう only expresses conjecture.
Wrongly dropping “の/ん”: with V/いA you need のではないか (not Vではないか).
Wrong intonation distorts the meaning: rising → question; falling → criticism/praise.
Using じゃないか in formal written language: choose ではないか / のではないか instead.

rows: Does not directly seek agreement; neutral
Softer and more objective than ではないか; used with clauses
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>すぎるのではないか。
Casual; sounds more feminine with rising intonation

examples: It is said that this area was once a wide field.
It is said that this festival has been held in the village since ancient times.
It is said that tofu came to Japan from China about 1300 years ago.
I hear that the next exam will be quite difficult.
I heard that the lecture will be canceled because the professor is attending an international conference.
I saw the news that a baby panda was born.
fields.explain:
NというN: used for naming, identifying or introducing. Natural, not too stiff.
文というN: puts the information of a whole sentence in to modify nouns such as噂・話・意見・考え・事実…
ということ／というの: nominalizes so the sentence can act as subject/object; more formal than っていうこと.
というのは: introduces a definition or explanation; what follows is the content that clarifies the meaning.
“～という”: at the end of a sentence it means “I hear/it is said that”, more formal than って.
Avoid overusing っていう in academic texts or written exams.

• Links content (a name, information, a clause) to a noun in the sense of “called/is called/is said to be/such as”.
• Before a noun: NというN or ClauseというN → “N (that is) called …”, “N (that) … is said to be …”.
• With ということ／というの: nominalizes a clause → turns the whole sentence into a “fact/thing”.
• というのは: opens an explanation/definition, close to “that is/meaning”.
• The spoken っていう makes sentences more natural in conversation, but avoid it in formal writing or official presentations.
• Nuance: neutral; “～という” has a sense of relaying transmitted information or naming objectively.
fields.notes:
• The preceding clause (before という) can be in the past, affirmative or negative: 来なかったという噂, 高くないという評価…
• ということだ can also mean “that means/the conclusion is”: 3割引ということだ → “that is, 30% off”.
• というより／というか: shifts or adjusts what was said; strong conversational nuance.
• Use brackets「…」+ という to quote a title or proper name exactly.
mistakes: Confusing ということ (nominalization) with と言う (to say that): ということ does not need an agent who “says” something.
Using っていう in JLPT N2/N1 writing: prefer という／とされる／とのことだ.
Missing “だ” before という with nouns/na-adjectives: 彼は元気だという噂 (do not drop だ in formal written language).
Confusing という with そうだ (hearsay): というN modifies a noun; そうだ cannot.
Using というのは without a following explanation leaves the sentence incomplete.

fields.explain: ◎ Used with the plural of people and things; it means「どちらも」.
fields.notes: Attaches to the 「－く」 and 「かろう」 forms of i-adjectives. In spoken language, 「－くても」 is the usual form. ① means 「そのように見積もっても」 and is followed by an expression estimating a quantity. 「多くとも１０人」「長くとも３０分」「遅くとも５時までに」 are similar usages. When 「－かろうと」 is repeated twice, as in ③, 「も」 is often omitted.

examples: I think this is wrong.
I'd like to become a doctor.
I think this plan is the most realistic.

fields.explain:
“～と思います” is polite and less imposing; used in meetings and discussions.
“～と思う” is neutral/spoken. Combine it with “たぶん/おそらく/きっと” to adjust the degree of certainty.
Intention: Vようと思う/と思っています. If the intention is formed right now:今から勉強しようと思う。

• Expresses a subjective opinion or conjecture: “I think that/I believe that”.
• With volitional verbs: ～ようと思う shows a momentary intention; ～ようと思っています shows an established intention.
• Negative: ～ないと思う (think that … not) vs ～とは思わない (do not go so far as to think …) differ in strength and emphasis.
• In spoken language, んです/けど is often added to soften the statement: ～と思うんですが…
fields.notes:
• In the first person, “私は” is usually omitted: 私は行くと思う → 行くと思う.
• “～だと思う” with na-adjectives/N: in conversation だ may be dropped, but keep だ in written exams.
• と here is the quotation particle, not a condition.
• Scope of negation: AはBだと思わない (do not think A is B) differs from AはBではないと思う (think A is not B) in focus.
meaning_vi: Expresses the speaker's thoughts and feelings.
examples: 1. ①　3月30日ごろだと　おもいます。
I think it's probably around March 30.
2. ②　はなさんは　来ないと　おもいます。
I think Hana won't come.
3. ③　ちょっと　ねだんが　高いと　おもいます。
I think the price is a little high.
4. ④　日本語と　英語と　どちら　かんたんだ　とおもいますか。
Which do you think is easier, Japanese or English?
mistakes: Dropping だ in the wrong place: 彼は医者だと思う (written). In spoken language both are possible: 医者だと思う／医者と思う.
Mistaking と for a condition: と here is always the quotation particle for 思う.
Intention: ～と思う vs ～と思っています → choose correctly according to the context, “right now” or “already decided”.
Negative: choose ～ないと思う or ～とは思わない to express the degree of negation that fits the JLPT question.

examples: I have to return this book to the library by tomorrow.
I had to clean my room, so I went home early.
Labor laws must be observed.
Application documents must be in Japanese.
Safety standards must be met at all times.
I have to submit the report by tomorrow.
fields.explain:
Strength: stronger than ～なくてはいけない in terms of normativity.
Politeness: ～なければ なりません in formal dialogue; past ～なければ ならなかった .
It can sound like a command; when speaking to a superior or a customer, consider switching to ～ていただけますか／～てください（softer, but no longer meaning “must”).
When stating rules or provisions, this is the precise choice.

• Expresses strong obligation required by laws, regulations or responsibility: “must/have to ...”.
• Formal, objective; suitable for policy documents, reports and public statements.
• Emphasizes the consequence of not doing it: breaking the law, failing to meet standards.
• The subject is usually an organization or individual bound by a standard; rarely used to give direct orders to the listener.
fields.notes:
• To negate an obligation, use ～なくてもいい／～必要はない, not the negative ならない.
• In headings and regulations, the contracted form without a subject is common: ～しなければならない。
• Two variants with the same meaning of obligation: ～なければならない ≈ ～いけない; they differ mainly in a stiffer or softer nuance.
mistakes: Forgetting “で” with N/na: ×日本語なければならない → 〇日本語でなければならない.
Confusing the nuance with べきだ in inference questions: べきだ ≠ legal obligation.
Wrong negative: ×行かなければならないくない → 〇行かなくてもいい／行く必要はない.
Using it directly to the listener sounds rude: switch to a polite request if the goal is to ask a favor.

fields.explain:
Humble self-reference:私 など ／私 などは … shows humility.
Contempt/belittling: あいつ など …（that guy…） has a contemptuous nuance; use it with care.
Strong negation: ～ など ない／ありえない emphasizes "no way".
In listing: AやB など means "etc." as examples, not an exhaustive list.
More formal than なんか／なんて; suitable for written language, documents and exams.

• Listing representative examples: "such as…, etc." Often used with や／とか for a soft listing.
• Nuance of belittling/contempt or humility: when attached to a word referring to oneself (私など), or when dismissing something as trivial or worthless.
• In written language, など can follow a clause (V辞書形など) to give an evaluation of an action or ability, often together with ない.
• Formality: neutral→formal; more polite than なんか／なんて.
fields.notes:
• In research and academic writing, など is often used to mark a non-exhaustive list: 例：温度、湿度、気圧など。
• With quantities/estimates: 10人など（about 10 people） is less common than ほど/くらい but does occur.
• Fixed phrases carrying an evaluation: ～するなどもってのほか（out of the question）.
mistakes: Using など with contempt toward the listener or a superior → impolite. Avoid: あなたなど…
Mistaking など for an exhaustive listing. In fact it gives representative examples, not the whole set.
Wrong combination with verbs: Vます＋など is unnatural; use V辞書形＋など／～するなど.
In a negative sentence, forgetting ない loses the "no way" nuance.

examples: This meat is tough and hard to eat.
Do you have any cups that are sturdy and hard to break?
These characters are too small and hard to read.
Those shoes don't slip easily, so they're good for mountain climbing.
There's something about him that makes it hard to ask him for things.
Oil stains are hard to remove with water alone.
fields.explain:
Used in advertising and product reviews:汚れにくい／壊れにくい／傷つきにくい.
When talking about feelings and relationships:言いにくい／聞きにくい express hesitation and delicacy.
Negative: ～にくくない（not hard to do）; Past: ～にくかった.
Combine with adverbs:非常に／かなり／ちょっと + ～にくい to adjust the degree.

• Expresses that “V is hard to do”, due to objective or subjective factors: technique, environment, properties of the target.
• Expresses a tendency or property: 見にくいデザイン（a design that is hard to look at）, 汚れが取れにくい（stains are hard to remove）.
• Different from “難しい”: ～にくい describes difficulty in performing a specific action V; 難しい means difficult in general.
• Compared with ～づらい: ～にくい is more neutral/objective; ～づらい leans toward the speaker's feelings (psychological or physical sensation).
fields.notes:
• Inflects like an い-adjective: にくい→にくくない／にくくて／にくかった… used flexibly in complex sentences.
• Avoid redundancy冗長: instead of とてもとても読みにくい, use 非常に/かなり + 読みにくい.
• When describing UI/UX: 見やすさ/見にくさ are measures of how easy or hard something is to read or see.
mistakes: Wrong form: × 読むにくい → ○ 読みにくい（drop ます）.
Confusing it with 難しい: generally “hard to solve” → 難しい; “hard to do V” → ～にくい/～づらい.
Expressing the negative: 読みにくくない（not hard to read）, not × 読みにくいない.
Confusing the nuance with ～づらい: psychological/hesitation → prefer ～づらい; physical/objective property → ～にくい.

fields.meaning: Nothing but…, all the time…, full of… (repeating one action / all of one kind)
examples: As you get older, your memory just keeps declining.
Over the past few years, life has only gotten harder.
Even the Japanese you worked so hard to learn will just keep slipping away if you don't use it.
Neither work nor my private life is going well. The stress just keeps building up, and I'm getting fed up.
Since I retired, my savings have done nothing but decrease.
If things go on like this, the damage will only spread.
fields.explain:
Tense, form : Usually present; the past is used to describe a tendency that continued up to a certain point in time.
Topic : Usually social phenomena, indicators, health conditions, costs…
Nuance : With the tendency meaning, usually negative or worrying; with the “all that remains” meaning, neutral or positive.
Not used with single, momentary actions that do not imply a tendency.

• One-directional tendency: Describes a state progressing in one direction (usually bad) that the speaker can hardly influence. Close in meaning to ～一方だ, but ～ばかりだ usually has a clearer negative nuance.
• All that remains (the last task): Everything is ready; the only thing left is to do V. Nuance of “having reached the final step”.
• Pragmatics: Often used in written language, news and commentary. Avoid it for strongly positive tendencies (～一方だ is more natural).
• Different from ～たばかりだ: ～たばかりだ = “just did…”, indicating a point in time; whereas ～ばかりだ = a tendency or the remaining task.
fields.notes:
• When you need to emphasize escalation: “～増える一方でなく、増えるばかりだ” – choose “ばかりだ” if you want a negative nuance.
• With abstract nouns: 不安・負担・圧力・赤字・被害・緊張 combine naturally with “増す/高まる/広がる＋ばかりだ”.
• “All that remains” often goes with these verbs: 残る・待つ・祈る・任せる・出発する・始める.
meaning_vi: 「いつも～だけで、ほかのもの・ことはない。」 よくないと思っていることを言う場合が多い。
Always only ~; there are no other things or matters.
Often used to talk about things one considers good.
examples: 1. 弟は毎日あきずにカップラーメンばかり食べている。
弟は毎日あきずにカップラーメンばかり食べている。=> My younger brother eats nothing but cup noodles every day without getting tired of them.
2. 寮では同じ国の人とばかり話さないで、いろいろな国の人と会話したほうがいい。
寮では同じ国の人とばかり話さないで、いろいろな国の人と会話したほうがいい。=> In the dorm, instead of talking only with people from your own country, you should talk with people from many different countries.
3. ありがとうございます。いつもいただくばかりで、お返しもできなくてすみません。
ありがとうございます。いつもいただくばかりで、お返しもできなくてすみません。=> Thank you. I'm sorry that I'm always just receiving and never able to give anything back.
4. 子どもはただ泣いているばかりで、何があったのかわからなかった。
子どもはただ泣いているばかりで、何があったのかわからなかった。=> The child did nothing but cry, so I couldn't tell what had happened.
5. この写真の女の子は今どうしているのでしょう。彼女の幸せを祈るばかりです。
この写真の女の子は今どうしているのでしょう。彼女の幸せを祈るばかりです。=> I wonder how the girl in this photo is doing now. All I can do is pray for her happiness.
explain: ◎ Indicates doing one thing many times, or having many of only one thing.
examples: 1. テレビばかり見ていないで、勉強しなさい！
Stop watching nothing but TV and study!
2. この辺はビルばかり建っていて、公園などはない。
There's nothing but buildings around here, and no parks or anything.
explain: An action is performed continuously
Something or someone exists in large numbers
examples: 1. この店のお客さんは、女性ばかりですね。
The customers at this shop are all women, aren't they?
2. 弟は、テレビを見てばかりいる。
My younger brother does nothing but watch TV.
3. 息子は仕事もしないで遊んでばかりいる。
My son doesn't work and just keeps playing around.
Increasingly…, nothing but… | Nothing but, all the time | All…, keep…, full of…
mistakes: Confusing ばかり and だけ: ばかり often has a critical nuance; in neutral sentences use だけ.
Vたばかり does not necessarily mean “immediately after”; don't translate it rigidly, as the JLPT often sets traps with relative time.
Confusing the two meanings of Vるばかりだ: rely on the context, “tendency” or “only the task remains”.
Confusing ばかり and だらけ: だらけ is used only for negative things, “full of/covered in”.
The structure しか～ない does not go with ばかり: ×しかばかり → incorrect.
